sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML text, PDF for figures)

steps.action: States the aim: assess the role of horizontal heat advection in snowmelt, both in a real-world snow patch and in an idealized DNS environment.
steps.quote: we aim to assess the role of horizontal advection of the sensible and latent heat in snowmelt

steps.action: Chooses the Finseelvi catchment (smooth topography, maritime climate, nearby flux tower) and a flat snow patch during the June 2019 melt as the field conditions.
steps.quote: makes the Finseelvi catchment a suitable location for assessing the influence of vertical turbulent heat fluxes on melting patchy snow covers

steps.action: Acquires daily photogrammetric images of the upwind and downwind edges over 11-15 June 2019, tower meteorology, and three snow-density samples from a pit on 14 June.
steps.quote: three snow samples were taken to determine the snow density

steps.action: Builds a low-cost SfM workflow (1087 smartphone images, MicMac, coregistered DEMs and orthoimages at 0.04 m) with a seven-step post-processing and filtering procedure, adapted from Filhol et al. (2019).
steps.quote: The height maps are obtained by applying the photogrammetric principle of structure from motion (SfM) using MicMac

steps.action: Takes the measurements of Harder et al. (2017) on a single 15 m snow patch as the basis of the idealized system instead of the authors' own field data.
steps.quote: Instead of using our own measurements, the idealized system is based on the measurements of a single snow patch done by

steps.action: Designs four DNS experiments (P15m, P30m, P60m at constant snow cover fraction 0.25, and a no-buoyancy P15m-NB), with parameters fixed by a Buckingham Pi dimensional analysis on the Moser et al. (1999) channel flow.
steps.quote: we doubled and quadrupled λ sn compared to a reference simulation with 15 m long snow patches

steps.action: Uses the MicroHH 2.0 DNS code, developed and shown to reproduce turbulent channel flow in a co-author's earlier work.
steps.quote: showed that MicroHH is able to reproduce this turbulent channel flow

steps.action: Sets the simulated conditions: an 1800 s neutral spin-up, then prescribed periodic snow and bare-ground buoyancy patterns generated from 2D power spectra in Fourier space.
steps.quote: At the bottom boundary, a pattern of surface buoyancies that depends on the simulation is prescribed

steps.action: Reports observed surface lowering of about 23 cm at the upwind edge and 3 cm at the downwind edge, with the downwind reference shifted to 12 June.
steps.quote: the snow surface decreased by approximately 23 cm, whereas for the downwind edge, this decrease was approximately 3 cm

steps.action: Estimates the melt error from the spread of stable bare-ground cells after vertical correction and propagates it to height differences.
steps.quote: allows us to estimate the melt with an error of ± 2.0 and ± 0.4 cm, respectively, for the upwind and downwind edges

steps.action: Compares the radiation-driven melt from Eqs. 1-2 (albedo 0.6-0.8) with the downwind melt and finds that the minimum radiation melt exceeds the observed melt.
steps.quote: The minimum estimated melt due to net radiation from 12 June until 15 June was 3.9 cm

steps.action: Attributes the downwind mismatch to uncertainty in the net-radiation estimate, keeping the assumption of negligible turbulent flux at the downwind edge.
steps.quote: so this mismatch is most likely caused by uncertainties in the net radiation estimates

steps.action: Infers the turbulent heat flux at the upwind edge as the energy-balance residual of observed minus radiation-driven melt.
steps.quote: we estimate these fluxes at the upwind edge to be between 73 and 102 ± 11 W m - 2

steps.action: Compares the inferred fluxes with Mott et al. (2018), Olyphant and Isard (1988) and Harding (1986).
steps.quote: [...] same order as those found in other studies in somewhat similar conditions

steps.action: Indicates a significant latent heat share from the specific-humidity difference, estimates a 60-80 % turbulent share of upwind melt, and extrapolates to at most about 10 % catchment-wide using Schlögl et al. (2018b).
steps.quote: we estimate the contribution of the turbulent heat fluxes to the snowmelt to be roughly 60 to 80 % for the upwind edge

steps.action: Runs the P15m DNS, which gives negative fluxes of about -500 W m-2 at leading edges, decaying downwind, and positive fluxes over bare ground.
steps.quote: The leading edge of the snow patch shows the highest fluxes towards the surface

steps.action: Runs P30m and P60m, which reduce domain-averaged snow heat fluxes by about 15 % and 25 % while the total flux is unchanged (Figure 6, p. 4332).
steps.quote: For the simulation with a quadrupled snow patch size (P60m), the heat fluxes are reduced by approximately 25 %.

steps.action: Sets the patch-size dependence against Schlögl et al. (2018a), which it contradicts, and Marsh et al. (1999), which it agrees with, and attributes the difference to ARPS resolution.
steps.quote: Our findings are more in line with the results of , who based their work on a 2D boundary layer model

steps.action: Fits a power-law decay of surface sensible heat flux with distance from the leading edge across all patches and runs (Figure 7, p. 4332).
steps.quote: the fluxes decay over distance from the leading edge according to a power law

steps.action: Compares simulated fluxes with the field-derived fluxes: about 5 times larger at the upwind edge, and the simulated decay is too weak relative to the near-zero downwind contribution.
steps.quote: [...] the upwind edge, the simulated sensible heat fluxes are approximately 5 times larger than the derived contribution of the combined turbulent heat fluxes

steps.action: Attributes the mismatch to the idealized forcing (Harder conditions, no nighttime melt) rather than revising the simulated mechanism.
steps.quote: the simulations are based on highly ideal conditions for turbulence-driven melt and local-scale advection of sensible and latent heat

steps.action: Uses the no-buoyancy run as an ablation: the decay is unchanged and only leading-edge flux magnitudes differ.
steps.quote: suggesting that stability has little influence on the decay of the surface heat fluxes, i.e., shear turbulence dominates

steps.action: Excludes wind speed (constant along the patch) and roughness (uniform by design) as causes of the decay, leaving the decreasing IBL temperature gradient (Figure 8, p. 4334).
steps.quote: Wind speed, another important component affecting the sensible heat flux, remains constant over a snow patch

steps.action: Compares simulated horizontally advected heat (Eq. 17) with Harder et al. (2017): higher values, and the observed reduction downwind is not reproduced.
steps.quote: This reduction is not found in the comparable simulation with a similar dominant snow patch pattern.

steps.action: Recomputes advected heat with a 4 m instead of 2 m integration height, which then matches the surface flux and gives the same -0.35 decay.
steps.quote: When considering a 4 m integration height, the horizontally advected sensible heat is approximately equal to the vertical sensible turbulent heat fluxes

steps.action: Contrasts the -0.35 exponent with the up to -0.47 of the Granger et al. (2002) boundary-layer integration.
steps.quote: through boundary-layer integration, our advected heat decays less

steps.action: Lists auxiliary limitations (low Re_tau, wind and temperature scaling inaccuracies, no roughness contrast or topography), declines a direct simulation-observation comparison, and qualifies the power law.
steps.quote: should be approached with caution

steps.action: Keeps the field estimate of a 60-80 % turbulent share at the upwind edge, at most about 10 % catchment-wide.
steps.quote: the snowmelt at the upwind edge is estimated to be between 60 % and 80 %

steps.action: Keeps the simulation claims: a constant power-law decay caused by air cooling over the patch, and lower mean fluxes for larger patches.
steps.quote: Domain-averaged sensible heat fluxes even reduced by 15 % and 25 %

steps.action: Expands the literature context (energy-balance models, Marsh 1997/1999, remote sensing) at the referee's request.
steps.quote: We will include a more elaborate discussion of the amount of research done regarding this topic.

steps.action: Rewrites the SfM post-processing description as an explicit seven-step procedure.
steps.quote: We agree that the text describing the SfM, and especially the post-processing of the DEM and orthoimages can be better formulated.

steps.action: Defends the strict cell filter by reporting that looser filters give unrealistically wide height changes; this check appears only in the rebuttal.
steps.quote: when loosening these filters, the size of the boxplots increases drastically, also to unrealistic values

steps.action: Declines to add the latent heat flux to the DNS and keeps the sensible-only design.
steps.quote: we chose to only consider the sensible heat flux to explore the potential of using DNS for studying this kind of system

steps.action: Adds caveats on the applicability of the power-law scaling relationship as a parametrization.
steps.quote: In a revised version, we will better emphasize our concerns about the applicability of the formulated relationship.

steps.action: Specifies snow-density sampling (pit, 100 ml at three depths, 14 June) and argues the snowpack was ripe; corrects the SWE/density confusion.
steps.quote: The samples were taken by digging a small snow pit and collecting 100 ml samples at 5, 25 and 45 cm below the surface

steps.action: Agrees to contrast the power law with Granger et al. (2002) and Weismann (1977); the comparison appears in §5.3 ¶6.
steps.quote: Thank you for this suggestion, we are currently looking into this.

steps.action: Referee asks for runs at higher Re; no new runs are made and the final paper only recommends them for future work.
steps.quote: have you run any simulations with a higher Re in line with Harder 2017

steps.action: Computes horizontally advected heat from the DNS with Harder's Eq. 2 to separate it from the vertical surface flux (becomes Eq. 17 and Figure 8c).
steps.quote: For this comparison, we will use equation 2 from Harder et al. (2017), which will also be referred to in our revised version.

steps.action: Declines to rerun the DNS with field-matched boundary conditions and keeps the Harder et al. (2017) forcing, with justification.
steps.quote: due to the absence of accurate local meteorological measurements at the snow patch, we decided to use the data reported by Harder et al. (2017)

steps.action: Adds a comparison with Schlögl et al. (2018a) and a discussion of the benefits and drawbacks of DNS.
steps.quote: we will include a discussion on how our study relates to Schlögl et al. (2018), also treating the benefits and drawbacks of DNS

steps.action: Declines whole-patch photogrammetric coverage because of equipment limits.
steps.quote: However, this would require other equipment than what was available.

steps.action: Clarifies the albedo range and adds the Harding (1986) source for it.
steps.quote: The values are based on Harding (1986), who did measurements in the same region

steps.action: Declines a fetch-distance analysis of melt and keeps treating the edges as points.
steps.quote: we treat the observed height change at the both edges as “point” data, due to the small coverage area

steps.action: Relates the 60-80 % upwind share to the catchment scale via Schlögl et al. (2018b), giving the at-most-10 % estimate in §4.1 ¶2.
steps.quote: state how these numbers relate to snowmelt on catchment scales

steps.action: Declines terrain-resolving radiation modelling as out of scope.
steps.quote: it would be out of scope to consider this in the study we present here

steps.action: States the auxiliary assumption of approximate atmospheric equilibrium over the patchy cover, so that the residual flux is attributed to local advection.
steps.quote: we do assume that the atmosphere has adapted itself to the patchy snow cover and is approaching equilibrium

tree.answer: Wind-driven advection enhancing leading-edge melt of patchy snow, known from prior studies
Melt observed directly by SfM; turbulent contribution not observable, inferred as energy-balance residual
Quantify the field contribution and explain flux behaviour and patch-size dependence with idealized DNS
No stated rival hypotheses; candidate causes of the decay (temperature gradient, wind speed, roughness, stability) examined in simulation
Partly: the no-buoyancy run separates stability effects; wind profiles separate wind from temperature-gradient effects
Set in DNS (patch size, buoyancy); found in a single field campaign

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: No: one patch, one five-day campaign
Partly: survives patch-size, no-buoyancy and integration-height variation; Re and forcing not varied; mismatch with field and Harder decay
Kept: power-law decay and size-dependent mean flux, to be approached with caution
Revised after two referees; several requests declined (latent heat, higher Re, field forcing, spatial melt)

end.claim: In idealized DNS (patch sizes 15-60 m, fixed snow cover fraction and stability), sensible heat flux into snow decays from the leading edge as about x^-0.35 because the air cools over the patch, independent of patch size, so mean fluxes fall by about 15 % and 25 % when the typical patch size is doubled and quadrupled.

decisive_move.sentence: The DNS runs with doubled and quadrupled patch size at constant snow cover fraction produce the 15 % and 25 % flux reductions and the size-independent decay; without them there is no patch-size claim.

gates.evidence: Field acquisition was aimed at the upwind and downwind edges, reflecting the leading-edge expectation, but no hypothesis is stated (§2 ¶2). The field residual could have shown no turbulent contribution, and the simulated decay was compared with the field data and with Harder et al. (2017); both mismatched, and the mismatches were handled by protecting auxiliaries (§4.1 ¶2, §5.3 ¶2, §6 ¶5). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen; the 50 cm outlier threshold and filter choices are post hoc.

imports.item: Moser et al. (1999) turbulent channel flow at Re_tau 590 as spin-up and reference
Random-phase Fourier synthesis with inverse FFT for periodic surface patterns

novelty_claims.quote: As this is one of the first studies to use DNS to investigate the role of the vertical turbulent heat fluxes and local heat advection [...]
estimates of a multiple-day contribution of the turbulent heat fluxes to the melt of a single snow patch are lacking

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: the field turbulent share (60-80 % upwind, at most about 10 % catchment-wide) is estimate_with_resolution, with ranges driven by the albedo assumption; attributing field melt to the simulated mechanism is best_explanation at most, stated as expectation (§6 ¶3); the low-cost SfM workflow is capability_characterized (errors ±2.0/±0.4 cm). Composition is none_fits: the walk is a single-site energy-balance estimate followed by idealized simulations forced by another site's data (Harder et al. 2017); there are no stated rivals, no crucial test, and no repetition by nature. The simulated decay disagrees with both the field data and Harder et al. (2017), and the paper protects the auxiliaries (Re_tau, scaling, ideal forcing) rather than testing them. Re_tau and forcing were not varied, and latent heat was not simulated. The 10 % catchment figure rests on relations from Alpine sites. The radiation overestimation from topography (§4.1 ¶3) is noted but not quantified. The loosened-filter robustness check appears only in the rebuttal (AC1 ¶10), not in the paper. Inference: dates of the field and simulation work relative to each other are not reported, and it is unclear whether the simulation design preceded the field campaign.

disagreements.support: The DNS gives 15 % and 25 % flux reductions for doubled and quadrupled patch size, against the minor size effect reported from ARPS.
disagreements.quote: This is in contrast to the results [...] .

disagreements.support: Argues that coarse resolution cannot resolve the thin stable IBL and that the Monin-Obukhov assumptions are violated, which DNS avoids.
disagreements.quote: Potentially, the differences from are caused by the inability of ARPS to fully resolve the leading edge effect

disagreements.target: Numerical ABL models and large-eddy simulations relying on horizontal homogeneity
disagreements.support: States that their assumptions are violated over patchy snow, motivating DNS.
disagreements.quote: these assumptions are violated for a patchy snow cover, thus introducing a large uncertainty

disagreements.support: Simulations forced by Harder's conditions give higher advected heat and do not reproduce the observed reduction to about 20 % over the next 4.8 m.
disagreements.quote: This reduction is not found in the comparable simulation with a similar dominant snow patch pattern.

disagreements.target: Granger et al. (2002) boundary-layer integration power law
disagreements.support: Simulated exponent of -0.35 against their up to -0.47.
disagreements.quote: through boundary-layer integration, our advected heat decays less

disagreements.target: Mott et al. (2018) and Harding (1986) on negligible latent heat flux
disagreements.support: High measured humidity gradients (at least 0.9 g kg-1) imply a significant latent contribution at Finseelvi.
disagreements.quote: For our observations, however, it is expected the latent heat flux also had a significant contribution from the high relative humidity
